summary.summary: Derbyshire held borrowing flat at £400.9m in 2025/26 but the mix leans on short money: £124.5m is short-term borrowing from other local authorities (average maturity 0.2 years) and 33% of all debt matures within 12 months, in a market where year-end inter-authority rates spiked to 5-7%. Internal borrowing rose £69m to £302.8m as usable reserves fall — partly because reserves are being used to fund the DSG schools deficit — and the forecast balance sheet assumes an £84m SEN refund from government in 2026-27. Investment income strongly overachieved (£10.9m vs £3.9m budget) and the £11.4m Buxton Crescent Hotel loan was repaid in full when the hotel was sold in December 2025. The £50m nominal strategic pooled funds still carry a stated £4.455m unrealised loss behind the statutory override (extended to April 2029), with a £3.9m reserve held against it; all prudential indicators were complied with.

signals.headline: Usable reserves are being used to fund the DSG deficit, lifting the net borrowing requirement from £286.596m to £356.906m at 31 March 2026; forecast balance sheet resources include an estimated £84.051m SEN refund in 2026-27 and £43.689m in 2027-28 and 2028-29
signals.why: The schools deficit is converting into real borrowing need, and the recovery path leans on government refunds that have not yet been received.

signals.headline: 33% of £400.929m borrowing matures within 12 months at 31 March 2026, including £124.500m of short-term local authority loans at 4.46% (WAM 0.20 years; £117.5m taken and £138.0m repaid in year); the report records year-end short-term LA rates of 5.0-7.0%
signals.why: A third of the debt book rolls over annually in the inter-authority market, whose price spiked at exactly the time of year the council refinances.

news_drafts.headline: Derbyshire Council fails to meet accounts deadlines for second year running
news_drafts.lead: Derbyshire County Council has failed to publish its draft financial accounts by the statutory deadline for the second consecutive year, triggering auditor concern about "potentially significant weakness" in its financial reporting arrangements. The 2025-26 accounts were due on 30 June 2026 but were not published until 14 August; the previous year's accounts were similarly delayed to November 2025. The auditor will now investigate whether the recurring delays were accompanied by material errors, poor working papers, inadequate resources or significant audit adjustments. The missed deadlines come as the council faces multiple unfunded budget pressures: its High Needs school funding deficit is forecast to reach £173.8m by March 2027, with services including children's placements and adult care forecasting combined overspends of over £7m and "Red" rated savings judged unlikely to be delivered.
news_drafts.paper_title: Derbyshire County Council - Audit Progress Report - September 26

findings.headline: Local government pay award remains ungreed for grades below Grade 17 and Grade 21, creating payroll cost uncertainty
findings.detail: The National Employers' pay offer of 3.3% has been agreed only for Grades 17-20. Grades up to 16 and Grade 21 remain in negotiation. The council budgeted for 3.5% increases and currently assumes this will be required for the ungreed grades.
findings.matters: Unresolved pay settlements create payroll forecast uncertainty and could exhaust the contingency buffer if final agreements exceed the assumed 3.5% for ungreed grades.
findings.quote: The pay offer has been agreed for points covered by the Council's Pay Grades on Grades 17 to 20. However, it has not yet been agreed for Grades up to and including Grade 16, or for Grade 21.

findings.headline: £2.5m of planned operating model savings are not being delivered in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council budgeted £2.5m for operating model savings but forecasts nil achievement. No explanation is provided for why these planned efficiency improvements have not materialized, and the paper does not indicate whether they have been postponed or abandoned.
findings.matters: Operational efficiency savings that fail to materialize affect the council's ability to deliver financial sustainability, particularly if the underlying budget pressures that required these savings are still present.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care holds 69% of outstanding receivables with over a third aged beyond one year
findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Health represents £25.372m of £36.768m total outstanding debt (68.9%). Of this, £8.590m (33.8% of ASCH receivables) is aged 1-2 years or older, indicating material collection challenges in this major service area. ASCH write-offs of £0.381m in the year (82.6% of all council write-offs) demonstrate recurring uncollectable receivables despite stable trend levels over the preceding four quarters.
findings.matters: A finance director must understand whether stated receivables will actually convert to cash; a lender must assess real cash position and collection risk in major budget areas.
findings.figures: £25.372m ASCH debt (68.9% of total), £8.590m aged 1+ years (33.8% of ASCH), £0.381m written off in 12 months

findings.headline: Demand-led financial assistance budget includes contingency to reduce support if demand exceeds available funding
findings.detail: Community Resilience Fund and DDF base budget for financial assistance total £10.3m and are described as demand-led. The council explicitly identifies a management approach that includes reducing support levels if demand exceeds the fixed budget allocation.
findings.matters: A willingness to reduce support if demand rises suggests the council treats the financial envelope for these services as fixed. Financial assistance services are typically needed more in economic downturns; a cap on support availability represents a constraint on the council's ability to respond to rising need.
findings.figures: £10.3m for Community Resilience Fund and DDF financial assistance in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Community Resilience Fund and the DDF base budget for financial assistance are demand led and total £10.3 m for 26/27. Careful management of these funds includes the potential to step down the level of support if demand exceeds funding.

findings.headline: Unfilled vacancies driving over £0.6m underspend across public health services in Q1
findings.detail: Multiple public health services showing vacancy-related underspends in the first quarter: Prevention services £0.257m, Financial Inclusion/Welfare Rights £0.240m, Community Safety £0.175m, and Needs and Intelligence £0.260m. Together these underspends account for the majority of the portfolio's £0.735m underspend.
findings.matters: Relying on unfilled vacancies to manage the budget suggests recruitment difficulties or delayed staffing plans. Support services operating under capacity could impact service delivery. If vacancies are filled later in the year, the budget will face pressure.
findings.figures: Prevention £0.257m underspend (vacancies and projects), Financial Inclusion/Welfare Rights £0.240m underspend (vacancies), Community Safety £0.175m underspend, Needs and Intelligence £0.260m underspend
findings.quote: Projected underspend of £0.240m in Financial inclusion/Welfare Rights due to vacancies, Prevention projected underspend £0.257m (vacancies and projects). DDF on budget.
